# 13 · AWS with boto3: unattached volumes, tag compliance, safe stop

*Sample output: what the model solution actually produces, on the input shown.*

## The main problem: EC2 hygiene

The account, as moto sees it:

```text
vol-0attached    100 GiB  attached to i-0tagged
vol-0orphan500   500 GiB  available (nothing is using it)
vol-0orphan8       8 GiB  available

i-0tagged        running     Owner, Env, CostCenter
i-0halftagged    running     Owner only
i-0untagged      running     no tags at all
i-0terminated    terminated  fully tagged
```

`find_unattached_volumes(ec2)`:

```python
    vol-0orphan500    500 GiB   <created first>
    vol-0orphan8        8 GiB   <created 1s later>
```

Reading that: only the two `available` volumes come back, and the attached one is
filtered out server-side rather than in Python — fewer bytes over the wire, and it
scales to an account with 40,000 volumes. That 500 GiB orphan is roughly €50 a month
for nothing. Oldest first, so the longest-running waste is at the top.

`find_instances_missing_tags(ec2, required={'CostCenter', 'Env', 'Owner'})`:

```python
    i-0halftagged    missing ['CostCenter', 'Env']
    i-0untagged      missing ['CostCenter', 'Env', 'Owner']
```

Reading that: the fully tagged instance is absent, as is the terminated one — a
terminated instance costs nothing and cannot be tagged, so reporting it is noise, and a
compliance report full of noise is one nobody reads. The untagged instance has no
`Tags` key at all in the API response, not an empty list, which is exactly the case a
naive `instance['Tags']` would crash on.

`stop_instances(...)`, which defaults to a dry run:

```python
stop_instances(ec2, targets, dry_run=True)  -> ['i-0halftagged', 'i-0untagged']
    (nothing was stopped: AWS reports a successful dry run by RAISING DryRunOperation)
stop_instances(ec2, targets, dry_run=False) -> ['i-0halftagged', 'i-0untagged']
    states afterwards: {'i-0halftagged': 'stopped', 'i-0untagged': 'stopped'}
stop_instances(ec2, [], dry_run=False)      -> []
    (an empty list never reaches the API: on many EC2 calls it means EVERYTHING)
```

Reading that: the dry run returns the ids it *would* stop, because with `DryRun=True`
there is no success response to inspect — the happy path lives in the `except` block.
Only `DryRunOperation` is treated that way; `UnauthorizedOperation` is re-raised, or the
safety check would cheerfully report 'would succeed' for a call your role cannot make.

## The variant: S3 audit

Three buckets, set up differently:

```text
prod-backups      versioning Enabled    SSE-KMS      all four public-access flags on
legacy-dumps      never configured      none         no public access block at all
marketing-assets  versioning Suspended  SSE-KMS      three of four flags on
```

`audit_buckets(s3)`:

```python
    legacy-dumps       ['versioning-disabled', 'no-default-encryption', 'public-access-not-blocked']
    marketing-assets   ['versioning-disabled', 'public-access-not-blocked']
    prod-backups       []
```

Reading that: `prod-backups` is clean. `marketing-assets` is flagged because
`Suspended` is not `Enabled` — versioning that was turned off still leaves you without
recovery — and because three of four public-access flags is not protection; `all()` of
the four or it doesn't count. `legacy-dumps` trips every rule.

A caveat this drill states honestly: moto reports a brand-new bucket as having no
default encryption, but since January 2023 real AWS applies SSE-S3 to every new bucket,
so `no-default-encryption` rarely fires in production. The rule worth shipping is
'not SSE-KMS with our own key', which `prod-backups` would pass and a default-encrypted
bucket would not.

`stale_objects(...)`, with `now` set 100 days after the objects were written:

```python
stale_objects(s3, 'prod-backups', prefix='logs/', older_than_days=90, now=NOW)
    logs/app-001.gz    1,048,576 bytes
    logs/app-002.gz    2,097,152 bytes
    logs/app-003.gz        4,096 bytes

stale_objects(s3, 'prod-backups', prefix='logs/', older_than_days=200, now=NOW)
    -> []
```

Reading that: at a 90-day cutoff all three log objects are stale, because they are 100
days old; at 200 days none are, and an empty list is the correct answer for a cleanup
job to do nothing with. `reports/q3.pdf` never appears either way — that is the
`prefix` filter doing its job server-side, so a bucket with a billion keys doesn't have
to be listed in full. `now` is a parameter rather than `datetime.now()` precisely so a
test, or a sample like this one, can pin it; it must be timezone-aware, because S3
returns aware timestamps and comparing aware with naive raises TypeError.
